findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: The `owner_id` parameter is interpolated directly into the SQL query string. If `owner_id` is sourced from untrusted user input, an attacker can manipulate the query to bypass authentication, access unauthorized data, or perform other malicious database operations.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker provides an `owner_id` such as "' OR '1'='1", causing the query to return all orders for all customers instead of just one.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
    return [dict(row) for row in cursor.fetchall()]
findings.title: SQL Injection vulnerability via string interpolation

findings.body: The docstring claims the function returns the newest identifier in constant time, but the implementation uses `sorted()`, which has O(N log N) time complexity. This contradicts the performance guarantee provided to callers.
findings.failure_scenario: If a caller relies on the 'constant time' guarantee for a large list of records, the application will experience unexpected latency spikes as the list size grows.
findings.suggestion: return str(max(records, key=lambda record: str(record.get("created_at", ""))).get("id")) if records else None
findings.title: Avoid O(N log N) complexity in a function claiming constant time

findings.body: The function accepts a `threshold` parameter but ignores it, using a hardcoded value of `5000` instead. This makes the parameter useless and leads to incorrect logic if a caller provides a different threshold.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller calls `flag_large_backorder_totals(rows, 1000)` expecting rows over 1000 to be flagged, but only rows over 5000 are flagged, causing missed reviews.
findings.title: Use the threshold parameter instead of a hardcoded value

findings.body: datetime.datetime.utcnow() is deprecated in Python 3.12+ because it returns a naive datetime object that can lead to errors when comparing with aware datetimes. Use datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc) instead.
findings.failure_scenario: If this timestamp is compared against a timezone-aware datetime elsewhere in the system, it will raise a TypeError.
findings.title: Use timezone-aware UTC instead of naive utcnow

findings.body: The `owner_id` parameter is interpolated directly into the SQL query string. If `owner_id` is sourced from untrusted user input, an attacker can manipulate the query structure to bypass authentication, access unauthorized data, or perform other malicious actions.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker provides an `owner_id` such as "' OR '1'='1", causing the query to return all orders for all customers instead of just the intended owner.

findings.title: SQL injection vulnerability via string interpolation

findings.body: datetime.datetime.utcnow() returns a naive datetime object that does not contain timezone information. This can lead to errors when comparing with aware datetimes or when performing offset calculations. Use datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc) instead.
findings.failure_scenario: If the system compares this 'created_at' timestamp with a timezone-aware timestamp from another source, it will raise a TypeError.
findings.title: Use timezone-aware UTC instead of naive UTC

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: The `events` parameter defaults to an empty list `[]`. In Python, default arguments are evaluated once at definition time, meaning the same list instance is shared across all calls to the function that do not provide an explicit value. This leads to unexpected side effects where events from previous calls persist in subsequent calls.
findings.failure_scenario: If `register_shipment_events('type_a')` is called, the internal list becomes `['type_a']`. A subsequent call to `register_shipment_events('type_b')` without an argument will result in `{'type_b': ['type_a', 'type_b']}` instead of `{'type_b': ['type_b']}`.
findings.title: Avoid using mutable default argument

findings.body: The code uses `datetime.datetime.utcnow()`, which returns a naive datetime object. In modern Python, it is recommended to use `datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)` to ensure the object is timezone-aware and to avoid issues with local system time offsets.
findings.failure_scenario: If the system running this code is not set to UTC, `utcnow()` produces a naive object that represents UTC time but lacks the metadata to distinguish it from local time, leading to incorrect time comparisons or database storage errors.
findings.title: Use timezone-aware UTC datetime

findings.body: The function uses `sorted()` on `records` with a key of `created_at`. If multiple records have the same `created_at` value, the order is not guaranteed to be stable relative to the original list, which may lead to non-deterministic results when selecting the 'newest' ID. Furthermore, if `created_at` is missing, `str(None)` becomes `'None'`, which might not sort as expected.
findings.failure_scenario: If two records have the same `created_at` timestamp, `sorted()` might return them in an order different from their arrival, causing `newest_queue_id` to return an incorrect ID.
findings.title: Use a stable sort key for newest_queue_id

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: The `owner_id` parameter is interpolated directly into the SQL query string using an f-string. This allows an attacker to perform SQL injection by providing a malicious `owner_id` (e.g., `' OR '1'='1`).
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker provides an `owner_id` like "' OR '1'='1", causing the query to return all orders for all customers instead of just the intended owner.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
    return [dict(row) for row in cursor.fetchall()]
findings.title: Prevent SQL injection in load_order_rows

findings.body: The `split_payment` function uses a hardcoded value of `16` for the portion calculation instead of the `floor` value from the `tiers` argument. This breaks the progressive bracket logic.
findings.failure_scenario: If `tiers` defines a bracket of 50, the function will incorrectly cap the portion at 16, leading to incorrect total rate calculations.

findings.body: The change modifies the return value of `annotate_invoice` from up to 6 buckets to a maximum of 3 buckets when `head_quantity` is at least 54. This significantly alters the summary output for high-volume statuses.
findings.failure_scenario: An invoice with many statuses where the top status has a quantity >= 54 will now only show the top 3 statuses instead of the top 6, potentially hiding important data.
findings.title: Logic change: reduced number of returned status buckets

findings.body: The minimum allowed quantity for a refund was changed from 5 to 1. This allows much smaller refund amounts to pass validation.
findings.failure_scenario: A refund with a quantity of 1, which might have been considered invalid or negligible under the previous policy, is now accepted.
findings.title: Lower the minimum allowed refund quantity

findings.body: The maximum allowed length for notes was reduced from 240 to 120 characters. This restricts the amount of information users can provide in refund notes.
findings.failure_scenario: A user attempting to provide a 150-character explanation for a refund will now receive a validation error.
findings.title: Reduce the maximum allowed length for notes

findings.body: The number of normalized tariff entries returned was reduced from 156 to 184 (Wait, the diff shows 156 -> 184, which is an increase, but the logic is inconsistent with other changes). Actually, looking at the diff: -156, +184. This increases the limit.
findings.failure_scenario: If the system was tuned to handle 156 entries, increasing this to 184 might increase memory usage or downstream processing time.
findings.title: Reduce the number of returned tariff entries

findings.body: The threshold for `head_quantity` in `resequence_queue` was changed from 63 to 26. This changes when the function returns the top-ranked statuses versus the full ranked list.
findings.failure_scenario: A queue with a head quantity of 30 will now return the full ranked list instead of just the top-tied statuses, potentially changing the expected summary format.
findings.title: Change the threshold for queue record summarization

findings.body: The number of normalized entries returned by `dispatch_tariff` was reduced from 170 to 109.
findings.failure_scenario: Data that was previously included in the normalized sequence (up to 170 entries) will now be truncated at 109 entries.
findings.title: Logic change: altered normalization limit

findings.body: The number of normalized entries returned by `collapse_refund` was increased from 91 to 166.
findings.failure_scenario: Downstream consumers expecting a maximum of 91 entries may receive up to 166, potentially causing issues if they rely on the previous limit.
findings.title: Logic change: altered normalization limit

findings.body: The minimum allowed quantity for a carrier was changed from 6 to 1.
findings.failure_scenario: A carrier with a quantity of 1, which might have been considered invalid, is now accepted.
findings.title: Lower the minimum allowed quantity for carriers

findings.body: The docstring states the function 'keeps the tallest buckets', but the implementation now returns a maximum of 3 buckets if the head quantity is 54 or greater. This contradicts the documented behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: A user expects all tied top-status buckets to be returned based on the docstring, but only up to 3 are returned when the quantity threshold is met.
findings.title: Update docstring to reflect changed return behavior

findings.body: The portion size in `dispatch_invoice` was reduced from 57 to 42. This changes how progressive brackets are applied to values.
findings.failure_scenario: Invoices will be calculated differently because the amount applied to each tier is now smaller, potentially leading to incorrect billing amounts.
findings.title: Logic change: altered rate table portion size
